title: Instead of becoming a boy, Pinocchio secretly leaves with his friend Candlewick for the Land of Toys.
paragraphs: Naturally, Pinocchio immediately asked the Fairy’s permission to go around town inviting his friends: and the Fairy said:
“Go and invite your friends to tomorrow’s breakfast: but remember to come home before dark. Do you understand?”
“I promise I’ll be back within an hour,” replied the puppet.
“Be careful, Pinocchio! Children are quick to make promises, but most of the time they are slow to keep them.”
“But I’m not like the others: when I say something, I keep my word.”
“We shall see. If you disobey, it will be the worse for you.”
“Why?”
“Because children who don’t listen to advice from those who know more than they do always run into trouble.”
“And I’ve found that out!” said Pinocchio. “But I won’t make that mistake again!”
“We shall see whether you mean it.”
Without another word, the puppet said goodbye to his kind Fairy, who was rather like a mother to him, and went out of the house singing and dancing.

In just over an hour, all his friends had been invited. Some accepted at once and very gladly, while others needed a little persuading at first; but when they heard that the rolls for dipping in their milky coffee would be buttered on the outside too, they all ended up saying: “We’ll come too, to make you happy.”

Now you should know that among his friends and schoolmates, Pinocchio had one special, very dear friend whose name was Romeo; but everyone called him Candlewick, because his little body was thin, dry and lanky, just like the fresh wick of a night-light.

Candlewick was the laziest and naughtiest boy in the whole school: but Pinocchio loved him dearly. In fact, he went straight to his house to invite him to breakfast, and didn’t find him: he went back a second time, and Candlewick wasn’t there: he went back a third time, and made the journey for nothing.
Where could he find him? He searched here and searched there, until at last he spotted him hiding under the porch of a farmhouse.
“What are you doing there?” Pinocchio asked, coming closer.
“Waiting until midnight, to leave…”
“Where are you going?”
“Far, far, far away!”
“And I’ve been to your house three times looking for you!…”
“What did you want with me?”
“Haven’t you heard the big news? Don’t you know what good luck I’ve had?”
“What?”
“Tomorrow I’ll stop being a puppet and become a boy like you and everyone else.”
“Good luck to you.”
“So I’ll expect you at my house for breakfast tomorrow.”
“But I’m telling you I’m leaving tonight.”
“At what time?”
“Soon.”
“And where are you going?”
“To live in a country… that’s the best country in the world: a real paradise!…”
“And what is it called?”
“It’s called the Land of Toys. Why don’t you come too?”
“Me? Certainly not!”

“You’re wrong, Pinocchio! Believe me, you’ll regret it if you don’t come. Where could you find a better country for us boys? There are no schools there: there are no teachers there; there are no books there. In that wonderful country, nobody ever studies. There’s no school on Thursdays: and every week has six Thursdays and one Sunday. Just imagine, the autumn holidays begin on the first of January and end on the last of December. That’s the sort of country I really like! That’s how every properly run country ought to be!…”
“But how do people spend their days in the Land of Toys?”
“They spend them playing and having fun from morning till night. Then in the evening they go to bed, and the next morning they start all over again. What do you think?”
“Hmm!…” said Pinocchio; and he gave his head a little shake, as if to say: “I’d quite like to live that way myself.”
“So, will you come with me? Yes or no? Make up your mind.”

“No, no, no, and no again. I’ve promised my kind Fairy to become a good boy now, and I mean to keep my promise. In fact, as I can see the sun going down, I’ll leave you straight away and run home. So goodbye, and have a good journey.”
“Where are you rushing off to in such a hurry?”
“Home. My kind Fairy wants me back before dark.”
“Wait another two minutes.”
“I’ll be too late.”
“Just two minutes.”
“And what if the Fairy scolds me?”
“Let her scold. Once she’s had a good shout, she’ll calm down,” said that rascal Candlewick.
“And how are you going? Alone or with others?”
“Alone? There’ll be more than a hundred boys.”
“And are you travelling on foot?”
“The wagon that’s picking me up and taking me right into that wonderfully lucky country will be coming along here soon.”
“What wouldn’t I give for the wagon to come now!…”
“Why?”
“To see you all leave together.”
“Stay here a little longer and you will.”
“No, no: I want to go home.”
“Wait another two minutes.”
“I’ve waited far too long already. The Fairy will be worrying about me.”
“Poor Fairy! Is she afraid the bats will eat you?”
“But tell me,” Pinocchio went on, “are you really sure there aren’t any schools at all in that country?…”
“Not a sign of one.”
“And no teachers either?”
“Not a single one.”
“And you never have to study?”
“Never, never, never!”
“What a wonderful country!” said Pinocchio, his mouth beginning to water. “What a wonderful country! I’ve never been there, but I can picture it!…”
“Why don’t you come too?”
“There’s no point tempting me! I’ve promised my kind Fairy to become a sensible boy now, and I won’t break my word.”
“Then goodbye, and give my very best wishes to the grammar schools!… And the upper schools too, if you meet them on the way.”
“Goodbye, Candlewick; have a good journey, enjoy yourself, and remember your friends sometimes.”
With that, the puppet took two steps as if to leave: but then he stopped, turned to his friend and asked:
“But are you quite sure that every week in that country has six Thursdays and one Sunday?”
“Quite sure.”
“But do you know for certain that the holidays begin on the first of January and end on the last of December?”
“Absolutely certain.”
“What a wonderful country!” Pinocchio repeated, spitting with sheer delight. Then, making up his mind, he added in a great hurry:
“So, goodbye for real: and have a good journey.”
“Goodbye.”
“How soon will you leave?”
“Soon.”
“What a pity! If you were leaving in just an hour, I might almost be able to wait.”
“And the Fairy?”
“I’m late already!… And getting home an hour earlier or an hour later makes no difference.”
“Poor Pinocchio! And what if the Fairy scolds you?”
“Never mind! I’ll let her scold. Once she’s had a good shout, she’ll calm down.”

Meanwhile night had fallen, and it was quite dark: when suddenly they saw a little light moving in the distance… and heard the jingle of bells and a trumpet call, so small and muffled that it sounded like a mosquito’s whine.
“There it is!” shouted Candlewick, jumping to his feet.
“What is it?” Pinocchio asked quietly.
“It’s the wagon coming to pick me up. So, are you coming, yes or no?”
“But is it really true,” the puppet asked, “that children in that country never have to study?”
“Never, never, never!”
“What a wonderful country!… What a wonderful country!… What a wonderful country!…”
